title: Local AI Options
description: When and how to run AI models on your own computer — and whether it makes sense for you.

data.text: Most people use cloud AI tools — ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini. But a growing number of users run AI models locally on their own machines. Here is an honest look at when that makes sense, how to do it, and the real trade-offs.

Until recently, running AI on your own hardware meant a research lab, a powerful workstation, and a lot of patience. That changed fast. Open-weights model releases from Meta, Google, Alibaba, DeepSeek, OpenAI, and NVIDIA — combined with tools like Ollama and LM Studio that handle all the complexity — mean that a capable AI assistant running entirely on your laptop is now a realistic option for non-developers. This lesson helps you decide whether it is the right option for you, and shows you exactly how to get started.
What 'running locally' actually means

When you use ChatGPT or Claude, your message is sent over the internet to a server, processed by a large model running on thousands of GPUs in a data centre, and the response is sent back to you. When you run AI locally, the model file — typically 4GB to 40GB depending on its size — is downloaded once to your computer. Every query runs entirely on your own CPU or GPU. Nothing is sent anywhere. The model has no network connection during use.

data.caption: Cloud AI sends your data to remote servers. Local AI keeps everything on your own machine.

data.text: The local model is an open-weights model — one whose trained parameters have been publicly released by its developers. Meta's Llama 4, Google's Gemma 4, Alibaba's Qwen 3.x, DeepSeek V4.1, OpenAI's gpt-oss, and NVIDIA's Nemotron 3 are the major families. These are not toy models: the best small and mid-size open-weights models in 2026 handle writing, summarisation, coding, Q&A, and analysis well — though they still trail frontier cloud models such as GPT-6 Astra, Claude Fable 5.1, and Gemini 4 Argon on the hardest reasoning tasks.

data.text: Reasons to run AI locally

items: Complete data privacy — nothing leaves your machine, ever. Critical for confidential business data, client information, or sensitive personal use.
Works fully offline — no internet required, no downtime from service outages
No usage limits or subscription cost after hardware (run as many queries as you want)
Consistent behavior — model stays the same until you choose to update it
Ability to customize, fine-tune, and swap models freely
No terms of service concerns about what you paste in

data.text: The honest trade-offs

rows: ✅ Access to GPT-6 Astra, Claude Fable 5.1, Gemini 4 Argon, etc.

data.text: The capability gap deserves context. Local models are not as capable as frontier cloud models — but that gap only matters for tasks that require frontier capability. For writing assistance, summarisation, brainstorming, simple coding help, and answering questions from a provided document, a well-run 8B–12B local model handles the task well. The gap shows up most clearly in complex multi-step reasoning, long-context tasks (processing an entire book at once), and sophisticated code generation across many files. Knowing which category your work falls into tells you how much the trade-off matters for you.
The best tools for running local AI

cards.title: Ollama
cards.description: The easiest way to run open models locally (Mac, Linux, Windows). Free. Download and run Gemma 4, Qwen 3.5, Llama 4, gpt-oss, DeepSeek V4.1, and dozens more with a single terminal command.
cons: Requires some comfort with a terminal

cards.title: LM Studio
cards.description: Polished desktop app for discovering, downloading, and chatting with local AI models. Looks and feels like a chatbot interface. The best starting point if you have never run local AI before.
cons: Less flexible than Ollama for programming use

cards.title: Open WebUI
cards.description: A self-hosted web dashboard that connects to Ollama. Looks and feels like ChatGPT but runs entirely on your machine. Great for households or small teams sharing a local AI.

data.text: Step-by-step: getting started with LM Studio

LM Studio is the recommended starting point for anyone who has never run a local model before. It requires no terminal commands and walks you through model discovery and download in a familiar app interface. The following steps take roughly 10–15 minutes end to end, most of which is download time.

data.title: LM Studio first-run walkthrough
data.content:
1. Download LM Studio from lmstudio.ai and install it like any desktop application.

2. Open LM Studio. On the left sidebar, click the Search (magnifying glass) icon to open the model browser.

3. Search for 'Gemma 4' or 'Qwen 3.5'. You will see multiple results — look for a chat/instruct variant from a trusted publisher such as 'google', 'lmstudio-community', or 'bartowski'.

4. Click the download arrow next to the Q4_K_M variant. A 12B model is roughly 7–8GB — a good balance of quality and size for most machines with 16GB RAM.

5. Once downloaded, click the Chat icon in the left sidebar. Select your downloaded model from the dropdown at the top of the screen.

6. Start typing. The model runs entirely on your computer — no internet connection needed from this point.

If responses feel slow, try a smaller model: search for 'Gemma 4 4B' or 'Qwen 3.5 4B' (roughly 2–3GB at Q4_K_M) for faster performance on 8GB RAM machines.

data.text: Ollama: local AI for developers and power users

Ollama's main advantage over LM Studio is its OpenAI-compatible local API. Once a model is running in Ollama, any application or script that can talk to OpenAI's API can be pointed at your local model instead — with no code changes beyond the base URL. This makes it easy to build private AI-powered tools, automate workflows, or integrate local models into existing projects.

data.caption: Install Ollama and run your first local model in three commands.
data.code:
# Install (Mac / Linux)
curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh
# Windows: download installer from ollama.com

# Pull and run a model (downloads ~7-8GB on first run)
ollama run gemma4

# Other useful commands
ollama list                  # see downloaded models
ollama pull qwen3.5          # download Qwen 3.5
ollama pull qwen3-coder      # code-focused model
ollama pull gpt-oss:20b      # OpenAI's open-weight reasoning model
ollama rm gemma4             # delete a model to free disk space

data.caption: Use your local Ollama model from Python — no API key or internet connection required.

data.text: Hardware requirements

rows: Larger / mixture-of-experts (Llama 4 Scout, DeepSeek V4.1, Nemotron 3)
64GB RAM or a GPU with ample VRAM

data.text: A note on Apple Silicon: Macs with M-series chips (M1 through M5) have a meaningful advantage for local AI. Their unified memory architecture means the CPU and GPU share the same RAM pool, so a 32GB MacBook Pro can run a 20B–30B model comfortably — something that would require a dedicated GPU with similar VRAM on a Windows machine. If you are shopping for hardware with local AI in mind, Apple Silicon is currently the best consumer option per dollar for this use case. On Windows and Linux, a dedicated NVIDIA GPU with CUDA support dramatically accelerates inference over CPU-only operation.
Understanding quantization: why the same model comes in different sizes

When browsing LM Studio or Ollama's library, you will see the same model listed at multiple sizes with labels like Q4_K_M, Q5_K_M, or Q8_0. These are quantization levels — formats that compress a model's numerical weights to reduce file size and RAM usage. An 8B model at full precision uses about 16GB of RAM. The Q4_K_M version of the same model uses roughly 5GB, with quality loss that is nearly imperceptible for most tasks.

rows: Good — minimal loss for everyday tasks
Default choice: lowest RAM with solid quality
When you have a bit more RAM and want a quality step up
Fine-tuning or benchmarking — rarely needed for chat

data.title: Which quantization to choose?
data.text: Start with Q4_K_M. It is the best default for almost everyone — small enough to run on 8–16GB RAM machines, and high enough quality that most users cannot tell the difference from full precision in ordinary use. Only go higher if you have headroom and are doing quality-sensitive work.
Which model should you actually run?

The model family you choose matters as much as the size. Different open-weights families are trained for different strengths — general conversation, coding, multilingual use, or efficient small-size performance. The table below covers the most widely used families available in Ollama as of late 2026.

rows: Best all-round small model; strong multilingual and structured tasks
Excellent multilingual reasoning and coding; efficient at small sizes
Open-weight reasoning model with strong instruction-following
Long context and general chat; needs 32GB+ RAM
Specialized for code generation and debugging
Efficient reasoning; good for agentic workflows

data.text: If you are unsure which to choose: start with Gemma 4 12B or Qwen 3.5 8B. Both are widely tested, handle the broadest range of everyday tasks well, and fit comfortably on a 16GB machine at Q4_K_M. If your machine only has 8GB RAM and it feels slow, switch to Gemma 4 4B or Qwen 3.5 4B — they punch well above their weight for their size.
When local AI fits — real scenarios

data.title: Scenario: confidential document drafting
data.content: A consultant is drafting a strategy report using sensitive client financials. Pasting that data into a cloud AI tool raises data-handling concerns — even with enterprise privacy tiers. Running a local 8B model means all drafting assistance stays on the consultant's laptop. The model sees the client data only within the current session; nothing is logged, transmitted, or stored externally. For writing assistance and restructuring prose, the local model is more than sufficient.

data.title: Scenario: offline travel and fieldwork
data.content: A journalist is reporting from a region with unreliable internet access. They need AI help summarising interview transcripts and drafting article sections. A locally running 7B model on their laptop works identically with full signal or none. No dependency on connectivity, no subscription continuity risk, and the model is always available exactly as configured.

data.title: Scenario: experimenting without a subscription
data.content: A student wants to explore AI capabilities — testing prompts, building a simple chatbot script, comparing model outputs — without committing to a monthly subscription or sending their experiments to a cloud service. Ollama lets them download Qwen 3.5 8B once and run unlimited queries locally at zero ongoing cost. When they want to test a different model, they pull it in one command.

data.title: Best starting point for most people
data.text: Download LM Studio → browse for "Gemma 4 12B" or "Qwen 3.5 8B" → click download → start chatting. Takes about 10–15 minutes including download time. No terminal required.
Limitations worth knowing before you start

Local models have no internet access. They cannot search the web, retrieve live information, or read URLs you paste in unless you build that plumbing yourself (tools like Open WebUI have basic document-loading features that help). If you need a model that can look things up in real time, a cloud tool with browsing enabled is more appropriate.

Local models do not update automatically. Unlike cloud APIs that silently improve over time, the model on your drive is frozen at the version you downloaded. Significant quality improvements ship every few months in the open-weights ecosystem — worth checking for updated versions of your preferred model every quarter or so.

Context windows are smaller. Many local models now support 32K to 128K tokens, but frontier cloud models offer around 1M tokens. This matters if you need to process long documents — a full research paper, a large codebase, or a lengthy transcript — in a single prompt. You can work around this with chunking strategies, but it adds complexity.

data.title: Is local AI right for you?
points: ✅ Yes, if: complete data privacy is required and you have 16GB+ RAM
✅ Yes, if: you work offline frequently or need a consistent model version
⚠️ Maybe, if: you want to experiment with AI without subscription costs
❌ No, if: you need the best model quality and cloud privacy policies work for you
Start with: LM Studio + Gemma 4 12B or Qwen 3.5 8B — 15-minute setup, no terminal required
On 8GB RAM: use Gemma 4 4B or Qwen 3.5 4B — small, fast, surprisingly capable
Quantization: Q4_K_M is the right default — low RAM usage, minimal quality loss
Developers: Ollama's OpenAI-compatible API lets you drop local models into existing code
